pos: n. plural (those who overcome in battle or contest; here, overcomers of tribulation through another's love)
etymology: Latin conquirere, to seek out, acquire by effort — one who gains complete victory, especially in warfare.
biblical_def:
Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.

Paul has just listed tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword — the full catalogue of what might seem to separate a believer from Christ's love — and answers it with a single, startling word: not merely conquerors, surviving these things, but more than conquerors in the midst of them. The phrase through him that loved us is the hinge on which the whole claim turns; this is not stoic endurance or human resilience but victory accomplished entirely through another's love, won in the suffering itself rather than after it ends. More than conquerors describes people who are, at the very moment of apparent defeat, already triumphant, because the thing threatening to separate them has already been answered at the cross.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONQUER: one who gains victory by force or superior power; a victor, especially in war.
webster_full: CONQUER, v.t. To gain by force; to win or vanquish by physical or moral power.
CONQUEROR, n. One who conquers; a victor.
Paul's superlative more than conquerors intensifies the ordinary term.
Victory located in the suffering itself, not merely after its end.
Attributed entirely to Christ's love, not to human endurance.
scriptures: Rom 8:37
Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.
corruption_summary: Self-help resilience culture happily borrows more than conquerors as a slogan of personal grit, detaching it from Paul's own explicit source of the victory: through him that loved us, not through inner strength summoned by the sufferer.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to print more than conquerors on motivational material while quietly dropping the clause that defines it. Paul's phrase is not a tribute to resilience but a confession of utter dependence — the victory belongs to Christ's love, received, not achieved.

The corrective is to keep the full sentence intact: tribulation, distress, and sword remain genuinely terrible, and the conquering is not denial of their weight but confidence that Christ's love has already outweighed them, in them, not merely after them.
roots_summary: Greek hypernikomen, a compound coined or intensified by Paul from nikao, to conquer, with the prefix hyper-, over or beyond — literally to super-conquer, found nowhere else in Greek literature before this verse.
roots_lines: Conquerors here is Paul's own intensified coinage, super-conquerors.
It answers a catalogue of real, severe sufferings.
The victory is located within the suffering, not merely after it.
Through him that loved us names the entire source of the victory.
Confidence rests on Christ's love, not on human resilience.
usage: In all these things we are more than conquerors — victory within suffering, not after it.
Through him that loved us — the entire source of the triumph named.
A coined superlative found nowhere else before Paul used it here.

pos: n. (one who argues or reasons contentiously; a debater relying on human wisdom)
etymology: Latin disputare, to examine, debate, from dis- and putare, to reckon — one whose trade is argument and reckoning by human reason.
biblical_def:
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?

Paul's triple rhetorical question targets the full range of human intellectual pretension — Greek philosopher, Jewish scribe, professional debater — and declares all three obsolete before the cross. The disputer of this world names specifically the trained arguer, skilled in rhetoric and dialectic, the kind of figure Corinth's culture prized above almost anything else. Paul does not answer the disputer with a superior argument on the same terms; he answers with the preaching of Christ crucified, a message the disputer's own categories call foolishness, and insists that God has deliberately chosen this route to make the world's whole system of argumentative wisdom look exactly as empty as it is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISPUTE: one who disputes or argues; a controversialist; one skilled in debate.
webster_full: DISPUTE, v.i. To contend in argument; to debate; to altercate.
DISPUTER, n. One who disputes; a controversialist, especially a professional one.
In 1 Corinthians, representative of worldly intellectual pretension generally.
Grouped with the wise man and the scribe as obsolete before the cross.
Answered not by superior rhetoric but by the preaching of Christ crucified.
scriptures: Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
corruption_summary: Apologetics culture can slide into treating the disputer's own game — winning the argument on the world's terms — as the main task of evangelism, exactly the approach Paul bypasses by preaching Christ crucified instead of out-arguing Corinth's professional debaters.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to read this verse as a call to become a better disputer than the world's disputers, defeating clever arguments with cleverer ones. Paul's actual strategy is different: he refuses the disputer's own chosen battlefield entirely.

The corrective is not anti-intellectualism but right ordering: careful reasoning has its place (Paul himself reasoned in synagogues, Act 17:2), but the gospel's power was never meant to rest on winning the disputer's contest, and a church that forgets this risks trading the foolishness of preaching for exactly the wisdom of this world Paul says God has already made foolish.
roots_summary: Greek syzetetes, a joint-inquirer or debater, from syn-, together, and zeteo, to seek or examine — a term for the professional dialectician common in Greek intellectual culture.
roots_lines: Disputer names the professional debater of Greek intellectual culture.
Paul groups him with the wise man and the scribe.
All three are declared obsolete before the preaching of the cross.
God has deliberately made foolish the world's argumentative wisdom.
The gospel bypasses the disputer's contest rather than winning it.
usage: Where is the disputer of this world? — a rhetorical dismissal of human intellectual pretension.
Hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
Answered by the preaching of Christ crucified, not superior argument.

pos: v. part. (speaking directly against; opposing by denial, here joined with open blasphemy)
etymology: Latin contra-, against, and dicere, to speak — to speak against what another has said.
biblical_def:
But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.

Luke pairs contradicting with blaspheming deliberately, tracing the opposition's escalation from its root cause, envy, through disagreement, to outright blasphemy against the gospel itself. The crowd's size, not the content of Paul's preaching, is what provokes the reaction — filled with envy at the response Paul and Barnabas were receiving, the Jewish leaders move from contradiction to blasphemy in a single verse. The pattern is a recurring one across Acts: resistance to the gospel is frequently rooted not in careful theological objection but in wounded status and envy, with contradicting serving as the first, most respectable-sounding stage of a hostility whose real source lies elsewhere.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONTRADICT: to assert the contrary of what has been said; to deny; to oppose in words.
webster_full: CONTRADICT, v.t. To assert the contrary; to deny the truth of what is said.
CONTRADICTING, part. The act of denying or opposing in speech.
In Acts, paired immediately with blaspheming as its escalation.
Rooted explicitly in envy at the size of the crowd, not theological objection.
Represents the first, most respectable stage of a deeper hostility.
scriptures: But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.
corruption_summary: Debate culture tends to present contradicting as pure intellectual engagement, but Luke traces this instance back to envy at the gospel's success, a reminder that stated objections sometimes mask an unstated, less flattering motive.
corruption_paragraphs: It would flatter the opposition in Antioch to assume their contradicting was a careful theological response to Paul's content. Luke removes that possibility by naming the actual cause first: filled with envy, before any content is engaged.

The corrective is discernment about motive, not dismissal of all objection: not every contradiction is envy-driven, but Scripture itself records that this one was, and the pattern is worth watching for whenever opposition to the gospel's success arrives dressed as careful disagreement.
roots_summary: Greek antilegontes, speaking against, from anti-, against, and lego, to speak — paired here with blasphemountes, the escalation from denial to outright reviling.
roots_lines: Contradicting is traced by Luke back to envy, not theology.
It escalates in the same verse to open blasphemy.
The crowd's size, not Paul's content, provokes the reaction.
This is a recurring Acts pattern of status-driven opposition.
Stated objections can mask an unstated, less flattering source.
usage: Filled with envy... contradicting and blaspheming — motive named before content.
A recurring Acts pattern of status-driven resistance to gospel success.
A call to discern real motive behind stated theological objection.

pos: n. plural (those who plot together secretly against a ruler or authority)
etymology: Latin conspirare, to breathe together, from con- and spirare, to breathe — those joined in a single secret, hostile purpose.
biblical_def:
And one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom. And David said, O LORD, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.

This single sentence delivers the heaviest blow of Absalom's rebellion: Ahithophel, David's own trusted counsellor, has joined the conspirators. David's response is not a counter-plot but a prayer, immediate and specific — turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness — trusting God with the political crisis rather than his own cunning. The prayer is answered in the following chapters when Ahithophel's sound counsel is rejected in favor of Hushai's flattering but strategically disastrous advice, and Ahithophel, seeing his counsel overruled, takes his own life. Conspirators names the human plot; the chapters that follow show whose counsel actually governs its outcome.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONSPIRE: those who plot together secretly, especially against a ruler or established authority.
webster_full: CONSPIRE, v.i. To plot together secretly; to combine for an unlawful purpose.
CONSPIRATORS, n. plural. Those joined together in a secret, hostile plot.
Ahithophel, David's own counsellor, is named among them.
David's response is prayer, not a counter-plot of his own.
The prayer's answer unfolds through the following chapters' events.
scriptures: And one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom. And David said, O LORD, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.
corruption_summary: Crisis management instinct favors immediate strategic countermeasures, but David's first recorded response to news of betrayal among the conspirators is a prayer entrusting the outcome to God rather than a plan of his own devising.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be entirely understandable for David, upon hearing that his own counsellor had joined the conspirators, to immediately begin plotting a strategic response. Scripture records prayer as his first recorded reaction instead, specific and urgent but aimed at God, not at his own cleverness.

The corrective is not passivity — David does act, sending Hushai back as a counter-influence — but the ordering matters: dependence on God named first, strategy following after and subordinate to it, a pattern worth recovering whenever betrayal or crisis tempts reliance on cunning alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew qesher, a binding together, conspiracy, from a root meaning to bind or tie — the same root used elsewhere of political conspiracies throughout the books of Kings.
roots_lines: Conspirators names those secretly plotting with Absalom against David.
Ahithophel's defection is the heaviest single blow in the list.
David's first response is prayer, not immediate counter-strategy.
The specific prayer is answered through later chapters' events.
Dependence on God is named first, strategy following subordinate to it.
usage: Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom — the heaviest betrayal named.
Turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness — prayer as first response.
Dependence on God ordered before any strategic countermeasure.

pos: n. plural (devisers; those who originate new forms or methods, here of evil)
etymology: Latin invenire, to come upon, discover — one who devises or originates something not previously existing.
biblical_def:
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents.

This clause sits inside Paul's longest and most comprehensive catalogue of fallen human conduct, the climax of Romans 1's argument that suppressed truth about God produces a darkened, degraded mind. Inventors of evil things names a particular and chilling capacity: not merely committing known sins but actively devising new ones, applying human creativity and ingenuity, gifts meant to reflect the Creator's own inventiveness, to the manufacture of fresh forms of wickedness. The phrase indicts civilization's capacity for innovation specifically, refusing to let technological or cultural advance be assumed automatically good; the same creative capacity that builds cities and arts can, apart from grace, be turned toward inventing evil things never before imagined.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from INVENT: one who devises or originates something new; here, applied to new forms of wickedness.
webster_full: INVENT, v.t. To find out, devise, or originate something not before known or practiced.
INVENTOR, n. One who invents; a deviser or originator.
In Romans, specifically of devising new forms of evil.
Sits in Paul's climactic catalogue of fallen human conduct.
Indicts creative capacity itself when turned from God toward wickedness.
scriptures: Rom 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
corruption_summary: Progress narratives tend to assume human innovation and creativity are morally neutral or inherently good, but Romans 1:30 names a specific, sobering category — inventors of evil things — as one mark of a mind God has given over to a reprobate state.
corruption_paragraphs: It is common to treat human ingenuity as automatically a sign of progress, divorced from moral direction. Paul's list refuses that assumption, placing creative capacity itself, when turned toward wickedness, among the fruits of a darkened mind that has suppressed the truth about God.

The corrective is not suspicion of creativity itself, a gift reflecting the Creator's own image in man, but sober awareness that the same capacity for invention is morally directional, not neutral, and can be given over, as Romans 1 describes, to manufacturing fresh wickedness as readily as it can build and bless.
roots_summary: Greek epheuretas, from epi-, upon, and heurisko, to find — the same root behind the English word eureka, here turned to devising evil rather than discovery of good.
roots_lines: Inventors names active devisers of evil, not mere sinners by habit.
The phrase sits inside Romans 1's climactic catalogue of fallen conduct.
Human creative capacity itself is implicated, not exempted.
Innovation is treated as morally directional, not automatically good.
The same capacity that builds and blesses can manufacture fresh wickedness.
usage: Inventors of evil things — creative capacity turned toward wickedness.
Part of Paul's comprehensive catalogue of a darkened, reprobate mind.
A warning against treating human innovation as automatically good.

pos: n. plural (fabricators of falsehood; those who manufacture lies, here applied theologically)
etymology: Old French forgier, from Latin fabricare, to make, construct — applied figuratively to those who construct falsehoods as a smith forges metal.
biblical_def:
But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value.

Job levels this charge against his three friends, whose theology was not random error but constructed, built falsehood — a coherent, confidently argued system insisting that Job's suffering must prove hidden sin. Forgers implies deliberate fabrication, not innocent confusion: the friends have taken a true principle, that sin brings consequence, and hammered it into a false universal, that all suffering proves sin, applying their forged theology to Job's wounds like physicians of no value, worsening the patient while claiming to diagnose him. The verse stands as a permanent warning that confident, systematic, even sincerely-held theology can still be forged falsehood if it is built to explain away a mystery rather than to submit to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FORGE: to fabricate or construct falsely; applied to counterfeit documents, and figuratively to constructed lies.
webster_full: FORGE, v.t. To fabricate; to make falsely, as a document or coin; figuratively, to invent or contrive a falsehood.
FORGERS, n. plural. Those who construct or fabricate falsehood.
Job's charge against his three friends' confident theology.
Implies deliberate, systematic construction, not innocent error.
Paired with physicians of no value, a failed diagnosis worsening the patient.
scriptures: Job 13:4
But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value.
corruption_summary: Confident theological systems can themselves become forgers of lies when a true principle is hammered into a false universal, exactly the error Job's friends committed by insisting suffering always proves hidden sin.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to assume sincerity and theological confidence are sufficient guards against error. Job's friends were sincere, systematic, and entirely wrong, their forged theology constructed to explain away a mystery — innocent suffering — that Scripture elsewhere refuses to resolve so simply.

The corrective is epistemic humility before mystery: the book of Job as a whole never fully explains Job's suffering to Job himself, and the friends' forged certainty, however coherent, is condemned precisely for refusing the kind of restraint the text itself models.
roots_summary: Hebrew tophley sheqer, literally plasterers or smearers of falsehood, an image of applying a false coating over a wound rather than healing it — vivid and fitting beside the physicians of no value that follows.
roots_lines: Forgers names deliberate, constructed falsehood, not innocent error.
Job charges his friends with a confident but false theological system.
A true principle has been hammered into a false universal claim.
Physicians of no value pictures a diagnosis that worsens the patient.
The book of Job models restraint before mystery the friends refused.
usage: Ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value.
A confident, systematic, yet entirely false theology.
Sincerity and coherence are not guards against error.

pos: n. plural (those who lead others astray, especially in doctrine; deceivers who worsen over time)
etymology: Latin seducere, from se-, aside, and ducere, to lead — one who leads another away from the right path.
biblical_def:
But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.

Paul's warning to Timothy, written near the end of his own life, refuses any expectation that error simply plateaus; seducers shall wax worse and worse, a trajectory of decline, not stability. The phrase deceiving, and being deceived captures the self-reinforcing cycle at the heart of doctrinal corruption: the seducer is not a cynical outsider manipulating sincere believers from a position of clear-eyed knowledge, but is himself progressively taken in by his own lies, each deception compounding the last. The verse sits beside Paul's charge to Timothy to continue in the things he has learned, making plain that the remedy for a world of worsening seducers is not cleverness to outmaneuver them but faithful continuance in what has already been received.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SEDUCE: one who leads another astray, especially from truth, duty, or virtue, by deceit.
webster_full: SEDUCE, v.t. To lead astray; to entice from the path of duty or truth.
SEDUCER, n. One who seduces or leads astray, especially in matters of faith.
In 2 Timothy, characterized by worsening decline, not stability.
Both deceives others and is simultaneously self-deceived.
Answered by Timothy's charge to continue in what he has learned, not cleverness.
scriptures: But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.
corruption_summary: A static view of error assumes false teaching settles into a stable, manageable position, while Paul describes seducers on a worsening trajectory, themselves progressively deceived by the very lies they spread to others.
corruption_paragraphs: It is comforting to imagine that once a false teacher's error is identified, it can be contained at its current severity. Paul's wax worse and worse denies this comfort, describing an active, compounding decline rather than a fixed, stable position.

The corrective is Paul's own prescribed remedy, given in the verses immediately surrounding this one: continue thou in the things which thou hast learned, grounded in Scripture profitable for doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness — steady continuance, not reactive cleverness, as the answer to a worsening deceiver.
roots_summary: Greek goetes, sorcerers or impostors, paired with planontes kai planomenoi, deceiving and being deceived, a wordplay built on the same root, plane, wandering or error.
roots_lines: Seducers are described on a worsening, not stable, trajectory.
They deceive others while being themselves deceived.
The Greek wordplay binds deceiver and deceived to the same root.
Paul's remedy is continuance in received Scripture, not cleverness.
The cycle of error is self-reinforcing and actively compounding.
usage: Evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse — active decline, not plateau.
Deceiving, and being deceived — a self-reinforcing cycle of error.
Answered by faithful continuance in Scripture already received.

pos: n. plural (those who inflict torment or severe suffering, here as agents of judicial punishment)
etymology: Latin tormentum, an instrument of torture, from torquere, to twist — one whose office is to inflict such suffering.
biblical_def:
And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him.

This is the climax of the parable of the unforgiving servant: a man forgiven an incalculable debt by his master turns and imprisons a fellow servant for a trivial sum, and when the master learns of it, that servant is delivered to the tormentors till he should pay all that was due. Christ immediately applies the parable without softening it: so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses. Tormentors here is not incidental scenery but the parable's full weight: the refusal to extend forgiveness received is treated by Christ as inviting a judgment as severe as the original debt itself, a warning aimed at professing disciples, not outsiders.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TORMENT: one who inflicts torment; an officer appointed to administer severe punishment or torture.
webster_full: TORMENT, n. Extreme pain; anguish; also, an instrument of torture.
TORMENTOR, n. One who inflicts torment; a jailer or executioner of punishment.
In Matthew, the agent of judicial punishment for an unforgiven debt.
Climax of the parable of the unforgiving servant.
Christ applies the image directly to disciples who withhold forgiveness.
scriptures: And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him.
corruption_summary: A sentimentalized reading of forgiveness treats it as a pleasant suggestion rather than an urgent command, but Christ's own application of this parable names unforgiveness as inviting the same severity pictured in delivering a man to the tormentors.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to soften the parable's ending as hyperbole, disconnected from the plain application Christ gives it. He does not soften it: so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you is stated without qualification immediately after the tormentors are named.

The corrective is to let the parable's severity stand as Christ intended it: forgiveness received from God and forgiveness extended to others are bound together so tightly that withholding the second is treated as evidence the first was never truly grasped, with consequences as serious as the tormentors' office implies.
roots_summary: Greek basanistais, from basanos, a touchstone used to test metals, extended to mean torture used to test or extract truth — officers specifically tasked with such severe treatment.
roots_lines: Tormentors are the agents of severe judicial punishment in the parable.
The servant is delivered to them for an unpaid, incalculable debt.
Christ applies the image directly, without softening, to his disciples.
Unforgiveness is treated as evidence that forgiveness was never grasped.
The parable's severity is deliberate, not hyperbole to be explained away.
usage: Delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due.
So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you — the direct application.
Forgiveness received and forgiveness extended are bound inseparably together.

pos: n. plural (acts or instances of deception; fraudulent indulgences practiced openly)
etymology: Old French decevoir, from Latin decipere, to catch or ensnare — instances of leading others, or oneself, into false belief.
biblical_def:
And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you.

Peter's description of false teachers reaches a particularly unsettling detail: these are not secretive sinners hiding their corruption, but men who riot in the day time, feasting openly at the church's own love feasts while sporting themselves with their own deceivings. The phrase pictures self-indulgent delusion as a kind of game these men play with themselves, taking pleasure not only in sin but in the deceptions that excuse it, and doing so in full public view, embedded within the fellowship of believers rather than lurking outside it. Deceivings here names a corruption so brazen it has stopped bothering to hide, the mark of a conscience Peter describes elsewhere in the same letter as having eyes full of adultery, that cannot cease from sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DECEIVE: instances of deception; fraudulent delusions indulged in and enjoyed by the deceiver.
webster_full: DECEIVE, v.t. To mislead; to cause to believe what is false.
DECEIVINGS, n. plural. Instances or acts of deception, here self-indulged.
Describes false teachers sporting themselves with their own delusions.
Practiced openly, at the church's own feasts, not in secret.
Marks a conscience so corrupted it no longer hides its sin.
scriptures: And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you;
corruption_summary: A church culture that assumes false teachers must be secretive or obviously hypocritical can be caught off guard by Peter's description: men sporting themselves with their own deceivings openly, at the fellowship's own table, unashamed rather than hidden.
corruption_paragraphs: It is comforting to assume corruption in the church will announce itself through obvious secrecy or visible shame. Peter describes the opposite: brazen, daytime indulgence, feasting openly with the very believers being deceived.

The corrective is vigilance that does not rely on a false teacher's discomfort as a warning sign; Peter's spots and blemishes language calls the church to discern by doctrine and fruit, not merely by the presence or absence of apparent shame, since the men he describes have none left.
roots_summary: Greek apatais, deceits or delusions, from apatao, to deceive, cheat — here used reflexively of men entertaining themselves with their own delusions rather than merely deceiving others.
roots_lines: Deceivings names self-indulged, brazen delusion, not hidden deception.
Peter describes false teachers feasting openly at the church's own table.
The corruption is practiced without shame, in full public view.
Discernment by doctrine and fruit is required, not reliance on visible guilt.
This marks a conscience Peter elsewhere calls unable to cease from sin.
usage: Sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you.
Brazen, daytime indulgence rather than hidden corruption.
A call to discern false teaching by doctrine, not by apparent shame.

pos: n. (betrayal of trust; violation of allegiance owed to a king or ally)
etymology: Old French trecherie, from trichier, to cheat or trick — a deliberate violation of the loyalty one is bound to keep.
biblical_def:
And Joram turned his hands, and fled, and said to Ahaziah, There is treachery, O Ahaziah.

This is the cry of a king recognizing, one moment too late, that he has ridden out to meet an assassin. Jehu, newly anointed by God's own command to end the house of Ahab, approaches furiously, and Joram's question, Is it peace, Jehu? receives no answer except an arrow through the heart; treachery is his last word before he dies. The scene is deliberately uncomfortable, because the treachery Joram names is, from the narrative's own standpoint, the appointed instrument of God's long-pronounced judgment on Ahab's house (1Ki 21:21-24) — a reminder that God's providence can work through acts that look, and are, treacherous by ordinary human standards, without God himself becoming the author of the treachery's sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TREACHEROUS: violation of allegiance or confidence; betrayal of trust, especially by one professing friendship.
webster_full: TREACHEROUS, a. Violating allegiance or confidence; betraying trust.
TREACHERY, n. The act of betraying trust; perfidy; violation of loyalty.
Joram's dying recognition that Jehu has come as an assassin, not an ally.
The treachery serves, in the narrative, as God's appointed judgment on Ahab's house.
Providence working through sinful instruments without becoming their sin's author.
scriptures: And Joram turned his hands, and fled, and said to Ahaziah, There is treachery, O Ahaziah.
corruption_summary: A simplistic reading of divine providence can struggle with an episode where real, culpable treachery is simultaneously the fulfillment of God's own pronounced judgment, but Scripture holds both truths together without resolving the tension into either fatalism or moral indifference.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to resolve the discomfort of this scene by either excusing Jehu's treachery entirely because it was prophesied, or denying any divine purpose in it because the act itself is treacherous. The narrative does neither.

The corrective is the same compatibilist pattern found throughout Scripture (Gen 50:20, Act 2:23): Jehu's treachery is genuinely his own act, for which he remains accountable (2Ki 10:30-31 notes his own mixed record), while God's pronounced judgment on Ahab's house is genuinely fulfilled through it, the two truths held together rather than collapsed into one.
roots_summary: Hebrew mirmah, deceit, treachery, from a root meaning to beguile or betray — the same word used of Jacob's deceit of Isaac, here applied to political assassination.
roots_lines: Treachery is Joram's dying recognition of Jehu's true intent.
The act fulfills God's long-pronounced judgment on Ahab's house.
Jehu's treachery remains genuinely his own culpable act.
Divine providence and human sin are held together, not collapsed.
The pattern recurs throughout Scripture's account of sovereign providence.
usage: There is treachery, O Ahaziah — a king's dying recognition of betrayal.
The act fulfills, without excusing, God's pronounced judgment on Ahab's house.
Providence and genuine human culpability held together, not resolved into one.
